questions.stem: What counts as 'new technology' for a start-up business?

options.text: Only robots and artificial intelligence
Any technology the business could use in production, distribution or marketing
Only technology invented in the last year
Technology is not relevant to small businesses

questions.explanation: New technology for a business includes any tool, system or platform that could improve how the business makes products, delivers them, or reaches customers. It does not have to be cutting-edge — just new to this business.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 105–112 on technology and business

questions.stem: Match each technology to the business area it mainly affects.
questions.explanation: Technology can be applied to different areas of business: production (how you make things), distribution (how you get things to customers), and marketing (how you reach and attract customers).

questions.stem: Adopting new technology is always beneficial for a business with no risks involved.
questions.explanation: Technology brings both opportunities and risks. Risks include: high setup costs, a learning curve, technical failures, security concerns, and the possibility that the technology becomes outdated quickly.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 110–115 on risks of new technology

questions.stem: How could social media technology create an opportunity for a small local bakery?

options.text: It can't — social media is only for big companies
The bakery could reach customers beyond its local area and showcase products visually
Social media automatically bakes the bread
It replaces the need for a physical shop

questions.explanation: Social media lets even small businesses reach a wider audience, showcase products with photos and videos, build a community, and take orders online. It is a low-cost marketing tool that creates real business opportunities.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 105–112 on technology and business

questions.stem: What is a realistic risk of relying on an e-commerce platform to sell your products?

options.text: The platform might change its fees or shut down, affecting your sales
Customers will never trust online shopping
The platform will steal your products
There is no risk at all

questions.explanation: Depending on a third-party platform means you are vulnerable to their decisions: they could raise fees, change algorithms, or even close. This is a genuine business risk that needs a mitigation strategy.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 110–115 on risks of new technology

questions.stem: 'Using technology' is specific enough when describing how technology helps your business.
questions.explanation: You need to name the specific technology (e.g., 'Instagram for marketing', 'Square for payments', 'Shopify for online sales') and explain exactly how it helps your particular business.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 105–112 on technology and business

questions.stem: A business starts using QR codes on packaging that link to recipe videos. Which area of business does this affect?

options.text: Production — how the product is made
Distribution — how the product is delivered
Marketing — how the business engages customers
None of the above

questions.explanation: QR codes on packaging that provide extra content (like recipe videos) are a marketing strategy. They engage customers after purchase and build brand loyalty — this falls under marketing, not production or distribution.

questions.stem: When analysing a technology for your business plan, you should:

options.text: Only list the benefits
Explain both the opportunity it creates AND the risks it brings
Only focus on the cost
Copy what your competitors use without thinking about it

questions.explanation: A good technology analysis covers both sides: the opportunity (how it helps your business) and the risk (what could go wrong). This shows critical thinking, which is what the assessment is looking for.
